s19.slug: FRIDAY · 7:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE — THE LAST NIGHT
body: The rain gets to Del Playa a little after dark. It comes in off the water ahead of itself — a handful of fat drops on the porch roof, loud as thrown gravel, then nothing, then the rest of it — and by the time Jack is at the top of Sol’s stairs with the Carhartt dripping on the floorboards it has settled over the house for the night: a steady hiss on the shingles, and the gutter outside her window already running over at the corner and spattering the sill.

The house is theirs. Sol is in Ojai and Tomás is on a boat, and downstairs the old refrigerator comes on and goes off and that’s the only other voice in the place. Her door is open. The suitcase stands just inside it, zipped, with the airline tag already looped through the handle, the first one ready. The coat from State Street hangs on the closet door. Her carry-on sits open on the desk chair, and on top of everything in it, folded square with the collar tucked under, is his flannel from the Walk.

He came up the hill in the CREW sweatshirt under the Carhartt, not washed, and she has the Carhartt off him in the doorway and then the sweatshirt. “Mine till six,” she says, and pulls it on over her T-shirt. The cuffs swallow her hands. The hem comes to the middle of her thighs, over a pair of boxer shorts with lobsters on them, and she looks at him out of the neck of it like she’s just robbed him and wants him to know it.

Dinner is on the floor at the foot of the mattress: Lupe’s truck, carnitas and rice in foil and a cup of salsa verde with the lid taped shut, bought at five and cold by the time they get to it. That’s his fault. He kisses her in the doorway with the rain still in his hair, and she kisses him back, and by the time anybody remembers the foil the tortillas have welded themselves into a single tortilla. She peels them apart one at a time and holds each one up to the lamp to check it. They eat cross-legged with the foil spread on the floorboards, her back against the side of the mattress, and she eats the rice with her fingers because the truck forgot the forks and she says forks are a crutch.
Halfway through the rice the RAZR buzzes against his leg.

body.text: Landed. Celeste has fed Margot twice. Arturo wept at the curb. The king sends regards.

body: “Ted?” she says.
“They landed. Arturo wept.”
“Arturo always weeps.” She licks salsa off her thumb. “He drove Ted to the DMV for his learner’s permit and wept in the parking lot. Ted failed. Arturo wept again.”
He shuts the RAZR and pushes it face down into the front pocket of his jeans.

Her *Brideshead* is on the pillow, a used paperback with somebody else’s name inside the cover and a Ralphs receipt two-thirds of the way through it. She’s been reading it because he is. She never said so. It was on the pillow Wednesday with the receipt in Book One, and tonight the receipt is in Book Three.

“Julia picks the one person in the book who can’t argue with her,” she says, with her mouth full of cold rice. “God. She tells Charles it’s for God, and Charles can’t get God on the phone to check. It’s the coward’s breakup.” She points a forkless finger at him. “I’d know. I’ve done it with a *publicist*.”
Yesterday he spent an hour at Hale’s table on Julia, and nobody in the room came up with that. He doesn’t argue it back. He likes hers better.

When the foil is folded into a ball and thrown at the wastebasket and missed, she stands up on the mattress in the sweatshirt and the lobsters, and she isn’t Skye. Her chin comes down. Her eyes go flat and patient and fifty years older than the rest of her, and she points at the desk chair.
“Sit,” says Dell Harlan. He goes to sit on the end of the mattress. “No. *There.*” He sits in the chair, on top of her carry-on and his own flannel. “You’re a suspect.”
“What did I do?”
“I ask the questions.” She walks the length of the mattress and back, the springs complaining under her heels. “Where were you Tuesday afternoon at ten to four.”
“At a red light.”
“Doing what.”
“Driving.”

“You don’t drive. Somebody taught you stick in an empty lot and you stalled it till she ran out of voices.” She leans down until the neck of the sweatshirt hangs open and her face is level with his. “Doing *what*, at the red light.”
“Singing.”
“Singing *what*.”

He won’t say it. She waits him out, nose to nose, unblinking, the rain loud on the window behind her, and he lasts longer than he expects to and not as long as he needs to, and when he cracks it’s into a laugh that he can’t get back.
“That’s what I thought,” says Dell Harlan, and straightens up, and it’s Skye who sits down hard on the mattress with her knees pulled up inside the sweatshirt.
Her iPhone lights on the windowsill. She reads it and turns it around and holds it out for him.
*car at six. no hat. you are NOT a sheriff in the airport.*

“I sent her a picture of the hat,” Skye says. “Tuesday. I bought it at the coat place while you were reading the price tag on the coat. That was a mistake.” She drops the phone back on the sill. The hat, it turns out, is in the closet, upside down on the shelf over the coat, the size and color of a pan of brownies.

“My mother’s coming the second week,” she says. “She booked the room next to mine. She wants to be there to watch it rise. Like I’m a soufflé.” She pulls the cuffs down over her hands and holds them shut with her fingers. “Sixteen days. It’s seven thousand feet up and it snows and everybody on that crew is going to be waiting to see if Cassidy can be anybody else, and I’m going to walk into that kitchen in front of them on Monday morning and open my mouth.”
He waits.
“I’m scared I’m only good when I’m nice,” she says.

body.text: He thinks of Tuesday night: the girl on this mattress in a pile of socks who looked up at him from the pages and made him lose his place.
body.else: He thinks of his Facebook wall on Wednesday morning, and of Corinne on the phone that night calling it *off-message*.

body.text: “You made me want to apologize to a horse,” he says. “In socks. I couldn’t find my line.”
body.else: “You told your whole network where to put its strategy,” he says. “On my wall. In front of my mother. That wasn’t nice.”

body: She looks at him over the cuffs. Then she lies back across the mattress with her hair spread out on the sheet and her feet on his knees, and he comes off the chair and lies down beside her, and the lamp on the floor by the bed throws both their shadows up the white wall, big and slow, over the window and the rain on it.

body.text: “You told me I’m the good thing *now*,” she says, on her back, looking up at the shadows. “I looked it up. *Now* is a very short word.”
body.else: “You said *for now*,” she says, on her back, looking up at the shadows. “I’ve been carrying it around all week like a pebble in a shoe.”

body: She turns her head on the sheet and looks at him with her eyebrows up, the way she sets up a punchline.
“*For now*’s running out of room, Youngstown.”
He doesn’t laugh, and in a moment she doesn’t either. Her hand comes out of the cuff and finds his on the sheet and holds it, and that’s all. She asked on Sunday. She doesn’t ask again.

body.text: A thought starts up the stairs toward him — a kneeler, and a man behind linen, and his own voice two nights ago saying *I mean to* — and he doesn’t let it in: he reaches over her to the lamp on the floor and turns it off.

A thought starts up the stairs toward him — a hand rising in shadow on linen, a blessing where the other thing should have been — and he doesn’t let it in: he reaches over her to the lamp on the floor and turns it off.

A thought starts up the stairs toward him — a little yellow bulb in a wire cage, seen through blue glass from Ocean Road — and he doesn’t let it in: he reaches over her to the lamp on the floor and turns it off.

body: The room goes to the sound of the rain, and to the gray that comes through the curtain from the corner of Del Playa. He puts his hand in her hair. It’s still damp at the roots from her shower, and warm under that, and she turns her face into his palm and keeps it there, and on the roof the rain comes down and down.

s19a.slug: FRIDAY · 9:30 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — THE YES
body: In the dark she rolls to the edge of the mattress and finds the iPod on the floor by feel, and the little speaker comes on low: an organ that sounds like it was left out in weather, a drum machine set to a walking pace, and a woman singing a long way down the far end of it, slow enough to lie down to. Skye comes back to him and puts her head in the crook of his arm.

They kiss for most of the song with the rain on the window. It isn’t like any of the other times. There’s nowhere it has to get to and nothing it has to stop short of; she kisses him like there are sixteen days of it to get in and no hurry about any of them, her hand inside the collar of his T-shirt, her knee across his. Every so often the gutter at the corner of the window lets go of a whole gutterful at once and it slaps the sill, and she laughs against his mouth the first time and doesn’t the second.

Her T-shirt has ridden up under the sweatshirt, and his hand is on the bare small of her back, and her skin there is warm and a little damp from the room. She hooks one finger in his belt loop and pulls him closer by it, though there’s no closer to be had with their clothes on, and laughs at herself for trying. He can feel the laugh where they’re pressed together. He can feel everything where they’re pressed together. All week it has been in him like a held breath, since a red light on State Street, and it isn’t something he has to work out anymore. It’s just there, the size of him.

She has asked him for this every way a person can ask for anything. In December, point by point, with visual aids. In a hundred small ways since. At the top of her stairs on Sunday, straight out, before anything. Every one of those asks was hers.
He says her name. She stops, her mouth still close enough to his that he feels her breathing change, and in the dark he can just make out her eyes, open, on his.

choices.key: On the last night, in the rain, you asked her. You told her it’s yes.
response: He gives her back her own sentence, the one from the top of the stairs, word for word: he wants to have sex with her. Tonight. And then the part she didn’t get on Sunday. “It’s yes.”

She doesn’t move. In the dark he can see the shine of her eyes and the line of her cheek where the streetlight finds it, and nothing else, and she looks at him from that close without saying anything at all while the song on the floor goes on without them.
“Jack,” she says, slowly, like she’s checking the name is his and he’s the one in it. She puts her fingertips on his mouth, where the word came out, and leaves them there while she breathes.

choices.text: *Tell her you love her. Then ask her.*
choices.key: On the last night, in the rain, you told Skye you love her. Then you asked her.
response: She’s heard it before. She goes still anyway, every time, like it’s news. He tells her the rest in the same voice, without dressing any of it: that he wants her, tonight, all of it, nothing held back and nothing kept for later; that it’s yes; that he’s asking.
Her hand comes out of his collar and finds his chest, the fingers spread, over his heart, and she leans her weight on it, and under her palm his heart has a good deal to say about all of this.
“Say the second part again,” she says.
He says it again. Her fingers press at every word.

choices.text: “*For now* just ran out of room.”
choices.key: On the last night, in the rain, you asked her: *for now* just ran out of room.
response: She laughs, surprised out of her, right against his mouth — and then she stops, and pulls back far enough to look at him in the gray.
So he does, with nothing on it for her to applaud: he wants her. Tonight. He’s asking her. “Yes.”
She lies there looking at him with her hand on his jaw and her thumb at the corner of his mouth, and he can feel the next laugh in her and feel her not use it.

choices.text: *Don’t say it. Let her feel it.*
choices.key: On the last night, in the rain, you didn’t say it. You let your hands say it. Then you said yes.

response.text: He doesn’t say anything. He puts his hands on her hips, where they were on Sunday night, and his hands, which held the last inch for both of them, let go. He pulls her in against him, all of her, the whole length, and there’s nothing in his grip now that means *this far*.
response.else: He doesn’t say anything. He puts his hands on her hips and pulls her in against him, all of her, the whole length, and his hands stop holding anything back. There’s nothing in his grip now that means *this far*.

response: She understands before he can get her name out. He feels it go through her: her breath stopping, her fingers closing in his T-shirt, her forehead coming down against his chin.
He says her name anyway. Then he says the rest of it into her hair, so there’s no mistaking it for the rain.

s20.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — RAIN

body.text: *I love you* is still in the room, and her hand is still spread over his heart.
Her laugh is still in the room, the one she didn’t use.
Nothing has been said in the room yet but her name and one word.

body: She sits up on the mattress and lifts her arms over her head like a kid at bedtime, and he takes the sweatshirt by the hem and pulls it up and off her. It comes off inside out with her T-shirt caught up in it, both together, and her hair comes through the neck last and falls down around her shoulders full of static, crackling where it touches his wrist. She shakes it back. In the gray from the window she’s bare to the waist, and he has seen her like this before, in a bath, in daylight, and it doesn’t make any difference at all; he looks at her the way he did the first time, and she lets him look, and then she pulls his T-shirt over his head and throws it at the closet.

His jeans she undoes herself, kneeling up on the mattress with her tongue between her teeth, and when she gets them down and off they go over the edge of the mattress in a heap. The RAZR is in the pocket. He hears it hit the floorboards, and that is the last he hears of it.
The lobsters go last. She laughs at them on the way down, at herself for wearing them tonight of all nights, and kicks them off her ankle into the dark.
Then there is nothing on either of them, and the rain, and the mattress, and the rest of the night.

She pushes him down on his back first. She kisses him from the notch of his throat down the middle of his chest, slow, the ends of her hair dragging after her mouth, her hands spread on his ribs to keep him there, and when she gets low enough she takes him in her mouth, unhurried, long enough that his breathing goes ragged, long enough to make him say her name at the dark ceiling — and then she lets him go and comes back up the length of him and lies down on his chest, pleased with herself, her chin on her hands.
“Your turn,” she says. “Make it good. I’m leaving the state.”

He knows her body by now; he has had weeks to learn it and he’s been a good student. He puts his mouth to her throat, to the place under her jaw that makes her breath catch, to the hollow of her collarbone, to her breast, and her hand goes into his hair and holds his head there and he feels her heart start to go under his mouth. Her other hand finds him, slow, sure, her thumb unhurried, and he says something against her skin that isn’t a word in English or Italian. He goes down the length of her, kissing her stomach, the jut of her hip, and puts his mouth between her legs, and she lets him until her heels dig into the mattress — and then her fingers tighten in his hair and pull him back up.
“Not like that,” she says against his mouth. “Not tonight. Up here. I want you up here.”

It’s his first time ever, and she knows it. She has known for months, and she has never made him pay for it. He has thought about this for years, in general. In general, it turns out, leaves out the elbows. He gets his weight onto his forearms over her and puts his left elbow squarely down on a fistful of her hair, and she yelps, and he snatches it back and apologizes, and his knee slides off the edge of the mattress onto the floorboards, and for a moment the first time of his life is a man trying to get up off a floor in the dark.
She laughs. He laughs too, with his face down in her neck, helpless, and she wraps both arms around his back and laughs with him, her mouth at his ear, until the mattress shakes with the two of them.
“Hi,” she says, when she can.
“Hi.”

“Come here.” She draws him back over her by the shoulders and gets her hair out of the way herself, all of it, up over the pillow, and settles him with her hands on his hips. “There. Stay there. That’s it.” Her knees come up on either side of him. She reaches down and finds him and brings him to her, and he follows her hands, and her eyes are open on his, close enough to see.
And then he’s inside her.

It goes through him all at once and very slowly: the heat of her, closing around him, so much more than he imagined and nothing like what he imagined, slick and close and alive, and he goes still because he has to, because if he moves he’ll lose it, and she goes still with him. They lie joined. He can feel her breathing from the inside. Her hand comes up and settles on the back of his neck, warm, her fingers in the short hair at his nape. Neither of them says anything. On the roof the rain comes down steady and close, and the streetlight through the curtain lays the window on the wall in a long gray shape.
“I’ve done this before,” she says.
She keeps her eyes on his.
“It’s never been *this*.”

He has nothing to set it against, and he tells her so with his mouth almost on hers: this is the only one he’s got. She touches his face, the scar through his eyebrow, with her thumb. “Good,” she says. “Then it’s this one.”
He kisses her. She moves her hips under him, a small lift, and it takes the breath out of both of them.

At first they don’t have it. He’s too fast, and too careful, and too fast again; he doesn’t know how much he’s allowed to want. She doesn’t tell him. Her heels find the backs of his thighs and slow him, and then they lift and draw him deeper, and she rises to meet him, and somewhere in the third try or the tenth the two of them find it — a rhythm, theirs, nothing like the music on the floor and nothing like the rain, slow and then not so slow. The mattress creeps across the floorboards toward the wall. His hands are on her hips, and all they do now is pull her closer. Her fingers on his neck tighten every time he moves into her, and let go, and tighten.

He has lived in this body for eighteen years and never been this far inside it. Every part of him is here, nothing held back in some other room: the sweat starting at the small of his back, her breath on his cheek, the gray light in her loosened hair and the static still crackling in it when his hand goes through, the freckle on her hip under his thumb, the rain and the rain and the rain. She’s looking at him. She’s smiling at him while he moves in her, a small private smile with her lip caught in her teeth, like they’re getting away with something wonderful in a crowded room and only the two of them know it. He has never been so glad of anything in his life.
“Skye,” he says.
She makes a sound in her throat.
“Mary Catherine.”
Her eyes close for that, and open again. “Jack.”
He tells her he loves her with his mouth against her cheek, and she says it back against his, and says it again, the words running together with her breathing.

She takes one of his hands off her hip and brings it down over her belly and holds it there under her own, her fingers over his, showing him with the pressure of them, and he does what her fingers tell him while he moves in her. Her breath goes ragged. Her head goes back on the pillow and the streetlight catches the line of her throat, and the flush that comes up her chest, and her mouth open. She says his name and doesn’t finish it. Then it takes her — he feels it before he sees it, around him and under him, her body drawing tight and arching up off the mattress against him, her heels pressing hard into the backs of his legs, her fingers dug into his nape, a long low sound coming up out of her — and her eyes open, on his, through all of it.

He doesn’t last after that. He doesn’t try to. It comes up through him from the base of his spine, and he says her name, both of her names, into her hair, and everything in him goes toward her and keeps going, and she holds him through it with her arms around his back and her mouth at his ear saying *yes* and *yes* and *I’ve got you*.

After, he doesn’t move, and she holds him there. He lies on her with his face in her neck and her hair in his mouth and her heart going against his chest, fast, and slower, and slower. Her hands go up and down his back. Somewhere in there the song on the floor ran out, and he didn’t hear it go. The rain hasn’t let up at all. Downstairs the refrigerator comes on. The old house creaks in the wind off the bluff, down the length of its stairs, and settles.
“Hi,” she says, into his hair.
He can’t do better than that. He doesn’t try. “Hi.”

s20a.slug: SATURDAY · 1:30 AM · DEL PLAYA LANE, HER ROOM — AFTER
body: The rain has eased off to a fine, even hush on the shingles, the kind you only hear when you listen for it. The gutter at the corner of the window has stopped running over and just drips now, slow, on the sill. Somewhere down on Del Playa a car goes by on the wet street with its wipers going and no radio.

They are under the blanket, warm through now, the sheet kicked into a rope at the foot of the mattress. She’s lying along him with her head on his shoulder and her knee over his thigh and one hand loose on his chest, and he has his arm around her with his fingers in her hair, and every so often, for no reason, one of them moves just to feel the other still there.
He is completely, perfectly happy. He lies in the dark with it and doesn’t do anything to it at all.
“It’s set,” she says. “The alarm. Four forty-five. It’s been set for days. You don’t have to remember anything.”
“Okay.”
“You’re going to sleep through it.”
“Probably.”
“I’m going to kiss you goodbye and you’re going to say *mm*.”
“I’ll say something better than *mm*.”

“You won’t.” She lifts her head and looks for the sweatshirt in the dark, and finds it, inside out at the foot of the mattress with her T-shirt still inside it, and drags it up and drops it on his chest. “Sixteen days. Washed. And don’t sleep in it.”
“I wasn’t going to sleep in it.”

“You’re going to sleep in it every night,” she says, “and wash it the morning I land, and tell me you didn’t, and I’ll believe you.” She settles back down. “Your brother says you tell the truth even when it costs you.”
“My brother also says I sing like a goat.”
“At a funeral. Get it right.” She thinks about it against his collarbone. “I’m writing him about Carrillo. He deserves an eyewitness.”
“Don’t you dare.”
“In capitals. HORSE. WRESTLING. THE GOAT AT CARRILLO.” She laughs into his shoulder, low, at her own list, and he feels the laugh go through her down to her feet, and he holds her while it does.
The drip on the sill slows. She yawns hugely, against his neck, and doesn’t apologize for it.
“Dell Harlan says you’re free to go,” she says, mostly asleep.
“I’m staying.”
“She knows.”

She’s gone a minute later, suddenly, the way she always goes — her hand on his chest going heavy, her breath slowing against his throat and deepening, a little catch at the top of every breath, her knee still over his. He lies and listens to it. The rain on the roof. The drip on the sill. The refrigerator downstairs coming on and going off. Her breathing. He pulls the blanket up over her shoulder and puts his mouth against her hair.

He falls asleep without noticing he’s going. The last thing he knows is the weight of her, and the warmth of her all down his side, and his arms around her and hers around him, in the dark, in the rain, in the one place on earth he would choose to be.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Seventeen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone. The day after Christmas my whole family watched season two of her show. She was eighteen, in a blazer, on a dock. She’s good — Dad said so, and she says nobody says good. Nonna prays for Cassidy now. She bought Chesterton used on Ventura without knowing it was my book, and wants to know who picked midnight. The Monday after Christmas she called, and we talked till my phone died. New Year’s Eve she watched my ball drop on the East Coast feed at nine her time and texted, so she’d be at midnight with me. Then she had her own, at three in the morning mine, from a locked den in the hills. I told her I called Ted *Ted*. She says he’s right: that one’s hers. She has my flight home written on her hand. She read Matthew 2 because I said Sunday was Epiphany; Herod is a jealous showrunner. OFFICIALLY, in eyeliner, on a sign at the rope at Santa Barbara, in sunglasses at night. A girl from my flight filmed it, and by morning it was on a gossip blog. Skye put the still on her own Facebook herself. Her people wanted lunch: her mother, Debbie, who manages her, and her publicist, Corinne. The rules: no pictures, ‘a friend from school,’ February. Take the airport down. She took it down. There was a folder with my last name on it, and she pushed it back without opening it. At a gas station in Buellton she took the first picture of the two of us herself, at arm’s length, and put it up instead. Then she changed her status herself and made me say yes to it on her phone — the first thing anybody ever watched her do that nobody wrote. Monday she came to the Fishbowl and argued with me about a rose. My pie got her out of remedial math. Tuesday she taught me stick in an empty lot — a voice for every stall. I do a bad Frank. We argued Conan. She posted a picture of me stalling. The radio, at 2:31: Haiti. At midnight she took the picture down — not for Corinne. Wednesday in the Brick she explained the plates under Haiti from her Oceanography book, read me Milton off the front of *Frankenstein*, and fell asleep on my shoulder. At the Haiti table she borrowed Becca’s apron and was Cassidy for twenty dollars a name, and asked me where God was at 4:53. Met Laney. Met everybody. Corinne wanted a statement; she told her the girl at the table was right about the pictures, and hung up. That night she asked me to say one for them, from her. ‘Saturday.’ Thursday Margot interviewed her at the Anchor; she says I’m the same in every room. Saturday at dawn she taught me again, inside the Point. Still very bad at it. She posted it and kept it up. She came to Sully’s and learned the Who Dat. Laney took a shot at her; she had it handled, she says, and I didn’t let her finish, and she says she’ll reward that sort of behavior. In the Saab I told her some about Lena — that we were close in the fall. She said she can tell there’s a rest. She drove me to confession, and went back to Sully’s without me. Saturday night she read me Sunday’s Gospel off her phone. Three nights in LA: a fitting for the wedding episode — she’s not the bride, she checked. Tuesday she made me explain Massachusetts while I walked. The tornado took Sol’s swing. Wednesday she drove home with the top down in the rain and put the two of us up on Facebook, soaked. Thursday we argued the Supreme Court under one umbrella until it turned inside out. She’s been a corporation since she was twelve — Skylark Pictures; her mother named it. She wrote my brother, in capitals; Rudy says write the number big. Friday the sun came out, and she called the telethon as Skylark. Saturday she drove six hours to the Walk for Life, walked the whole thing arguing with me, and stood in front of Clare when a man started screaming. Sunday she came to Mass. I told her why I didn’t go up. Out past the break I told her what I know about the basement, which isn’t much, and about Nonna’s question and Danny’s. She’s the answer to both. She knows there’s more; she said that’s enough. She asked me to teach her Nonna’s prayer. Monday a blog found the back of my head; Gina knew Danny’s jacket before the commenters did. Corinne called her at six: every picture of us down until there’s a strategy. At noon in her room I was the one who didn’t want to stop, and she stopped it — for Sunday. She’d read up on confession to do it: I can’t walk in on Wednesday with a plan, and she won’t be my plan. Ask her again after she’s watched me go up. She asked me what I lose when I sit in the pew, and I told her: they pass the plate over you. She watched them do it on Sunday and didn’t know what she was watching. Then she took a picture of us without looking, and that night she put it up, captioned with Corinne’s own rule — *my friend from school.* At the lunch in Studio City her shoes stayed on. When they got to Danny she came back for that and nothing else, and said his number from memory. In the car she said she’s very good at fine. She heard me tell Ma *tomorrow*, and that I think she’s the answer, and took the picture down at the Las Posas exit without a word. Sol’s swing is up. I told her I don’t care, and she could tell. She’s stopping anyway. She wants Nonna to like her. Wednesday she said Theo and Laney were running lines. Wednesday night she was at the curb when I got home from confession. She asked if I went. Then, in the middle of a bit about a Supreme Court justice, I said it first. I didn’t know I was going to. She’d been carrying it since Monday, and she was going to say it first. She said it back. Thursday she took me to a fundraiser in the Palisades and never said what for — it didn’t occur to her anybody would mind. It was for Boxer: Corinne wanted me in the picture so the march would stop being a story. She saw my face across the room and asked twice. I told her it was fine — she came to my Walk and took the other side seriously, so I could stand in hers. So she went back in and got the whole room to argue with me, the real arguments, in Gil’s living room, for two hours, and made sure every one of them knew where I stand. We stayed till the end. At a taquería at the bottom of Sunset she wouldn’t post Corinne’s picture. She blew me a raspberry and posted one of us at the table instead: we agree on each other, and we’re not just friends from school. She’s a union member. Two of them. Her father was Pat Doyle, a juicer on the Meridian lots, gone since she was four. Then she said her name. Mary Catherine Callender-Doyle. Baptized at St. Mary’s in Lancaster, named for his mother. The only name she has that her mother didn’t give her. I sent the first two to Gina for Nonna. At three in the morning I made the picture my profile picture. She says I stole her art. She says happy looks good on me. Friday she argued Margot to a draw and went home to learn lines. Saturday at the Point I told her Nonna lit a candle for Maria Caterina. Saturday night on the bluff she kept her word: tomorrow. Sunday she sat in the same pew, in a cardigan she bought for Mass, and watched me go up, and knelt. That night she asked first, before anything. I told her it’s still no, for now. And that it’s closer than it’s ever been. She asked what question she’s the answer to. I told her Nonna asked me what makes me pray. She asked if she does. Yes. She wants to be the good thing, with the lights off. I stayed. Just sleep. Tuesday she booked a pilot: a sheriff’s daughter in a border town who isn’t nice to anybody, outside Santa Fe, sixteen days. I told her Theo asked me to New Orleans. She said go. I told her Friday’s hers. At the red light at Carrillo we sang the whole song at each other, top down, and a girl in the next lane filmed it. She didn’t share it. She wrote on my wall instead: bring the clean version next time. I told her I was sorry about Cassidy and her mother and the network. She kissed me and told me never to apologize for making her happy. Thursday she read Danny’s letter out loud, and took my flannel to New Mexico, and left me her sweatshirt. Friday it rained. She said *for now*’s running out of room. I asked her. We fell asleep in each other’s arms.
